editorial.headline: Self-Service Wholesale Is Nationally Open, but Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This broad, self-service wholesale activity permits 100% foreign ownership nationally, yet PMA registration is blocked in Bali under its permanent risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
For a foreign founder considering Bali, the immediate answer is blunt: this activity cannot be registered there as a PMA business today. The code covers self-service wholesale or cash-and-carry trading in a wide variety of goods without a particular product specialism. Prices are set in advance; buyers select and take their own goods, then pay at a cashier. Its defining feature is therefore the wholesale format itself: a broad, non-specialist assortment handled through self-service, rather than simply any enterprise selling many types of goods.

Nationally, the position is open. The activity is listed as TERBUKA for PMA and allows foreign ownership up to 100%. It is also open at every stated business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. The record therefore does not confine the activity to one category of operator or reserve it for a narrower scale. For an investor reading the national framework, the starting point is clear: PMA participation is permitted, and the national foreign-ownership ceiling is full. The cited basis for that national position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Bali does not simply inherit that national result. Its local status is BLOCCATO_CLASSE_RISCHIO, and the stated reason is specific: at the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope. That brings the activity within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities, recorded as applying from May 2026. The practical result is categorical for a foreign-owned registration on the island: despite being nationally open, this activity is blocked for PMA in Bali.

This is a distinction that needs to remain sharp in any setup decision. The national 100% ceiling describes the level of foreign ownership the national framework permits; it does not override Bali’s local, risk-based PMA restriction. Nor does national availability across Mikro through Besar alter the Bali outcome, because the Bali finding is tied to the stated OSS risk position at Besar scale across every scope. Taken together, the record supports one precise conclusion: this is a nationally PMA-open self-service wholesale activity, available across the listed scales with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling, but it cannot be registered as PMA in Bali under the island-wide permanent moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness is real, but it does not override Bali’s island-wide, permanent PMA block for Low and Medium-Low risk activities.
